planting.note: Dormant-seed in late fall onto bare, firm soil so winter freeze-thaw cycles break seed dormancy; this small cool-season bunchgrass greens up earliest of any Great Basin grass and goes summer-dormant by early July.

directions: Sandberg bluegrass is the small, fine-leaved matrix bunchgrass that fills the interspaces between big sagebrush plants across millions of acres of the Great Basin, greening up weeks before other grasses and curing to tan straw by midsummer. Deep, coarse fibrous roots make it exceptionally drought- and grazing-tolerant, and it is one of the first native grasses to recolonize disturbed sagebrush steppe. Use it as a low, textural groundcover grass between sagebrush-steppe wildflowers rather than as a lawn substitute, since it is summer-dormant and browns off completely by late June in dry years. Avoid summer irrigation, which favors weedy annual grasses over this native.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, sparsely vegetated, sandy or rocky disturbed ground in full sun; seed benefits from a winter chill and germinates best where competing vegetation is minimal.

directions: Giant blazingstar is a short-lived Great Basin native prized for its enormous, star-shaped, lemon-yellow flowers up to five inches across, each with a prominent brush of long stamens, opening in late afternoon and remaining open into the following morning to attract hawkmoths and other evening pollinators. It colonizes disturbed, sparsely vegetated slopes, roadcuts, and sandy washes throughout the sagebrush steppe, where its rough, sticky, silvery-green leaves cling readily to clothing and fur. Give it the leanest, most neglected corner of a dry rock garden or gravel bed, since rich soil and competition from other plants quickly crowd it out. It self-sows reliably where bare ground is maintained, behaving as a biennial or short-lived perennial.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or early spring into lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this short-lived perennial establishes quickly and often blooms its first year from a fall sowing.

directions: Hoary aster lights up the Great Basin sagebrush steppe in late summer and fall with masses of pale lavender to deep purple, daisy-like flowers held on diffusely branched, gray-hairy stems, blooming after most other sagebrush-steppe wildflowers have finished for the season. It is a short-lived perennial pioneer, quick to colonize disturbed shadscale flats, roadcuts, and sagebrush openings, and it is an important late-season nectar source for native bees, butterflies, and migrating pollinators. It thrives in lean, rocky or sandy soil and full sun, declining in fertile or regularly watered ground. Because individual plants are often short-lived, allow some seed to disperse each year to maintain a population in the garden.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto lean, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun so winter cold can break seed dormancy; this biennial-to-short-lived-perennial often flowers in its second season.

directions: Douglas' dustymaiden forms low mounds of finely dissected, cobwebby gray-green foliage topped by flat-topped clusters of small, pale pink to white tubular flowers through the warm months, a common and widespread sight on dry, rocky ground throughout the Great Basin sagebrush steppe and up into subalpine scree. The felted, silvery leaves give the plant excellent drought tolerance and a soft textural contrast to bunchgrasses and sagebrush in a dry native planting. It is an easygoing pioneer of disturbed and rocky sites, equally useful in a gravel garden, rock garden, or restoration seeding, and needs nothing beyond sun and sharp drainage. Avoid damp or fertile soil, which shortens the life of this naturally short-lived species.

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat and sow in spring into lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; as a legume it needs no fertilizer but benefits from a rhizobium inoculant where prairie clovers have not grown before.

directions: Searls' prairie clover is an upright, woody-based perennial legume of dry bluffs, lime-rich clay terraces, and sandy flats across the Great Basin and Intermountain West, producing dense, cylindrical spikes of rose-purple pea flowers from early to midsummer that are heavily worked by native bees. Deep, tough roots and nitrogen fixation let it thrive in the leanest soils with minimal water, making it a valuable addition to dry native pollinator plantings and restoration seedings alike. It tolerates alkaline and lime-rich soils better than most garden legumes. Once established it needs no supplemental irrigation and resents heavy, wet, or fertile ground.
sources: BLM Great Basin Native Plant Project

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Scatter seed in fall onto bare clay or hardpan at the lowest point of a seasonally flooded basin; germination follows winter inundation, with bloom concentrated as the pool shallows and warms in spring.

directions: Fremont's goldfields is a true vernal pool bottom specialist of California's Central Valley, carpeting the deepest, longest-inundated hardpan pool basins with sheets of small, bright yellow daisy flowers as the water recedes in spring, often alongside Downingia species in classic goldfields-and-blue displays. It germinates underwater or in saturated mud and requires the pool to dry completely by early summer to complete its life cycle and set seed, making it suitable only for a clay-lined or hardpan basin that floods each winter and dries each summer. It differs from the more upland-tolerant Lasthenia californica in its strict dependence on the deepest, wettest part of the pool cycle. Never irrigate in summer, when the plant has already senesced and set seed in the dry basin floor.
sources: CNPS Vegetation Program (Lasthenia fremontii - Downingia bicornuta Alliance)

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Scatter seed in fall onto bare mud in the drying margins of a seasonally flooded basin; this tiny annual needs saturated soil to germinate and a full dry-down afterward to complete seeding.

directions: Dwarf woollyheads is a diminutive, gray-woolly vernal pool specialist found as mats of tiny, upright, felted stems bearing small spherical flower heads tucked among leaflike bracts, typically growing in the moist, drying margins of vernal pools and seasonal wetlands across much of western North America. Its minute stature and unassuming flowers make it more of an ecological curiosity than a showpiece, but it is an authentic indicator species for a constructed vernal pool garden aiming for ecological accuracy rather than pure ornamental display. Grow it only in a basin or swale that floods in winter and dries completely by summer, sown alongside taller vernal pool associates like goldfields and downingia for a layered, naturalistic effect. It will not persist in soil that receives any summer irrigation.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Scatter seed in fall onto bare, saturated soil in a seasonally flooded low spot; it is among the earliest vernal pool annuals to flower, often blooming by midwinter in mild years.

directions: Common stickyseed, also called yellow carpet, is a low California vernal pool annual that is often the very first wildflower to bloom as winter turns to spring, spreading sheets of pale, soft-yellow daisy flowers across the margins and shallow basins of seasonal pools from Shasta County south into the San Francisco Bay Area and Central Valley. The ring of stamens exudes a sticky, viscous fluid that coats the pollen and seeds, giving the plant its common name and likely aiding seed dispersal in the mud. It depends entirely on winter rains filling a basin and a subsequent spring dry-down, making it suitable only for a clay-lined rain garden or constructed vernal pool rather than an ordinary flower bed. Combine it with other early vernal pool bloomers for an authentic succession of color through the wet-to-dry cycle.

subcategory: California native vernal pool wetland perennial

planting.note: Sow in fall into wet, seasonally flooded margins or a rain-garden basin in full sun; rhizomatous roots let it persist through summer dry-down better than most other vernal pool specialists once established.

directions: Vernal pool checkerbloom is a rhizomatous mallow of wet grassland, hog wallows, and the margins of vernal pools across California, producing showy panicles of pink to purplish five-petaled flowers up to an inch across from spring into summer. Unlike many of its strictly obligate vernal pool neighbors, its spreading rhizomes allow it to persist at the drier edge of a seasonal basin, often blooming early in the season alongside other pool-margin specialists. It performs best where winter and spring moisture is abundant and soil dries only gradually through summer, making it a good transitional species between a flooded basin center and the surrounding upland planting. Established clumps slowly spread by rhizome, forming loose colonies at the pool edge.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Scatter seed in fall into a seasonally wet basin or swale in full sun; it flowers latest of the common vernal pool annuals, after most of the basin has already dried, so site it where some residual moisture lingers into early summer.

directions: Needle-leaf navarretia is a small, aromatic, prickly-textured vernal pool annual with leaves cut into stiff, needle-like, white-hairy segments and compact clusters of funnel-shaped white to pale blue flowers that open in early summer, later than most other vernal pool annuals. It occupies the drying centers and margins of pools, wet meadows, and old fields throughout much of western North America, often one of the last native wildflowers still blooming in a basin as the surrounding ground has already cured to summer dormancy. In a constructed vernal pool garden it extends the bloom season after the showier spring species like goldfields and calicoflower have finished. Grow it in the same seasonally flooded, summer-dry basin as other vernal pool specialists, with no supplemental water once the pool has dried for the year.
sources: Burke Herbarium Image Collection (University of Washington)
